frames.narration: A transfer of 100,000 bytes over links of 1,500, 1,400 (a tunnel with 100 bytes of overhead) and 1,500. The sender announced an MSS of 1,460 in its SYN, based on its own 1,500 byte interface. Packet size is MSS plus 40 bytes of headers: 1,500.
Without a tunnel everything fits: 69 packets, 100 kB delivered. The handshake and small requests also fit through the tunnel, so the connection opens and looks healthy.
With the tunnel, the first full 1,500 byte packet reaches a 1,400 byte link with DF set. The tunnel drops it. Typically it sends back ICMP 'fragmentation needed' carrying the MTU 1,400.
Path MTU Discovery works: the sender drops its MSS to 1,360 and resends. One wasted packet and one round trip; 75 packets sent in total (74 of data), 100 kB delivered.

Now a firewall on the path drops ICMP. The sender never learns, retransmits the same 1,500 byte packet and it is dropped every time. 0 bytes delivered. A 1,000 byte response would still get through, which is why monitors based on small requests stay green.

Clear the DF bit instead and the tunnel fragments each packet into 2 pieces (at most 1,376 data bytes each): 138 fragments for 69 packets. It works, but at 1% fragment loss a 2-fragment packet survives 9,801 times in 10,000, not 9,900, and many firewalls drop fragments.

The clean fix is MSS clamping: the tunnel endpoint rewrites the MSS in the SYN to 1,360. The sender never builds a packet that is too big: 74 packets, 0 wasted, 0 extra round trips, and it works with ICMP still blocked.
